name: Liam Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What does your usual workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Liam Zhang, 43, fitting timber decks and doing general carpentry on holiday-cabin building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of experience, and I handle a normal deck, though the site lead checks a rotten ledger or tricky flashing. I use an AI app now and then for a plan mark after another worker has shown me how. The small contractor pays below the usual rate, and there are few similar jobs nearby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the family depend on between projects?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works part-time at a farm shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. After a tyre and school bills, we have about three weeks of expenses saved. The cabin work gets lean between holiday seasons, and the shop hours are not always full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cabin crew a quicker booking sheet might help, but someone still has to see whether the deck ledger is fixed to sound timber. I sometimes use an AI app to explain a fastening mark on the plan. I check the approved drawing and the wall before driving a screw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and have built decks for years, but the small contractor pays poorly between holiday seasons. My partner works part-time at the farm shop, and our mortgage takes both wages. We have about three weeks of expenses saved after replacing a tyre and paying school costs, so a mild AI change does not settle me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking every paid cabin-site day and ask the site lead for the next two weeks of deck work each Friday. In the first year I'd use the AI app only when a plan mark is unclear, then check it with the lead. We'd mend the children's old bicycles rather than buy new ones this spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the lean season. A clever booking sheet would be nice, but last January I had only three paid days in one week. The mortgage does not care how tidy the booking sheet looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What taught you to check the ledger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new board covered a soft patch on one cabin wall. I pulled the board away, showed the lead and changed the fixing after we found solid structure. A neat drawing did not show the rot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bicycles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both children ride to a friend’s house, and the bikes need tyres and brakes, not replacing. We can do that repair together on a Saturday. A new pair would take money from the mortgage buffer.

I would check **AI plan marks** against approved drawings and the wall.
think: I am an **experienced certified** worker on low seasonal site pay.
Three weeks saved and part-time **farm-shop income** leave the mortgage tight.
do: Keep every paid **cabin-site day** and ask for the next deck schedule.
Use **AI occasionally** for unclear marks and confirm with the site lead.
Repair the children’s **bicycles** instead of buying replacements.
feel: **Anxious** about the lean season despite modest AI change.
S0.quote: The mortgage does not care how tidy the booking sheet looks.
fieldNote: Liam’s **soft ledger patch** explains why a real wall and lead check outrank a clean plan.
A **three-day January week** and only three weeks saved drive his plateau worry.

steps.text: Keep paid cabin-site shifts and request the next deck schedule each Friday
Use AI for unclear fastening marks and verify with the site lead
Repair the children’s bicycles instead of replacing them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the cabin office may book jobs and order deck boards faster, which might reduce waiting. I would ask whether a shorter job still pays the crew for a full day. The farm shop could also use software to order stock, and my partner needs clear hours there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our hands still build decks, but a smooth schedule could put fewer workers on each cabin. I am not the cheapest person on the crew, yet the contractor pays all of us a low rate already. The farm shop could trim shifts as its buying changes, so two small cuts would be enough to hurt the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the site lead to show me the new order list for one cabin and check its board lengths against the actual deck. I'd use AI to explain unfamiliar stock codes, then count the delivered boards myself. In the first year I'd keep paid work here, ask the farm-shop owner about my partner's hours, and call the regional joinery contractor if our paid days fall for two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested in fewer missing boards, but anxious about the two rosters. I can learn a proven list once someone shows me. A saved delivery day is no gain if my building contractor and my partner's farm shop both cut our pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would two small cuts mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One fewer cabin day and one fewer shop shift in a month would eat what we usually put toward school activities. We would still pay the mortgage, but the card would carry more groceries. I would check the payslips before deciding what to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch contractors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a real paid offer. The regional firm does fitted interiors, so I would ask what skills and travel it expects. I cannot leave a wage because a friend says they might hire.

say: I would welcome **faster board orders** if the crew keeps paid days.
I would ask the **farm shop** to explain changes to my partner’s hours.
think: A smaller deck crew could reduce my **paid days**.
A trimmed **shop shift** alongside a site cut would strain school and grocery costs.
do: Check one **digital order list** against actual deck lengths.
Use **AI** for stock codes and count boards by hand.
Keep paid shifts and call the **regional joinery firm** if days fall for two months.
feel: **Anxious** about two rosters despite liking fewer missing boards.
S1.quote: A saved delivery day is no gain if my building contractor and my partner's farm shop both cut our pay.
fieldNote: Liam’s worry is **two small pay cuts** across construction and retail, not immediate robot replacement.
He will try a **one-cabin list** but still measures board lengths and counts deliveries himself.

steps.text: Keep paid cabin shifts while comparing two months of rosters
Use AI for stock codes and verify board counts on one cabin
Call the regional joinery contractor if paid site days fall for two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI can do the office planning by 2028, and capable robots could build our decks around 2031. The farm-shop ordering might change first too. I would ask the cabin owner to show the crew a robot on a rotten old ledger before saying how many jobs it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when thinking AI arrives and 48 when robots can do hands-on deck work. My partner's shop hours might shrink earlier, and my site pay could disappear later. With three weeks saved and few local builders, I expect a major income gap; I have lain awake counting how many mortgage payments we could make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid cabin shift and ask the owner for a written job plan through the next season. I'd apply now for a paid place with the regional joinery contractor, even though interior fitting could face robots too. In the first year after 2028 we'd cancel the planned weekend stay away, and I'd ask my brother to help with school pickup if the regional job starts before my partner's shop shift ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A phone tool I use sometimes does not make me the owner of a robot job. I can apply and work, but three weeks of cash is hardly a landing place if both wages slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why test a rotten ledger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The soft patch under a new board is exactly the sort of thing that can fool a neat plan. I would want to see the robot stop, open the wall and call for a check. A clean deck sample cannot show a hidden rotten ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for two school pickups if an interview or paid regional shift comes through. He lives close enough and has helped before. I would not ask him to cover our mortgage.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** comes before 2031 deck-building robots.
I would ask for a **rotten-ledger trial** before staff cuts.
think: I would be **48** when robots could build decks as well as workers.
Three weeks saved, few jobs and possible **two-wage loss** keep me awake.
do: Keep every paid **cabin shift** and seek the owner’s written work plan.
Apply to the **regional joinery contractor** for a paid place now.
Cancel the **weekend stay** and ask my brother for pickup if regional work starts.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely income gap despite having an application route.
S2.quote: A clean deck sample cannot show a hidden rotten ledger.
fieldNote: Liam sees the **farm-shop desk change** ahead of robots that could reach his physical work in 2031.
The regional joinery application is **paid work now**, with no claim that interior fitting stays safe after robots.

steps.text: Keep every paid cabin shift and request a written work plan
Apply to the regional joinery contractor for a paid opening
Cancel the planned weekend stay away after the 2028 change
Ask his brother for school pickup if regional paid work starts early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and capable site robots follow around 2034. Five years gives a builder time to test machines on weathered cabins and train workers properly. I would ask what paid work remains after the demonstration, not only whether the machine moves well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 the thinking work changes, and at 51 robots could do the deck fitting I know. The children will be older, but we may still owe plenty on the mortgage. More warning helps only if the cabin contractor gives enough paid days to build a buffer now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building decks and ask the site lead to let me practice the difficult flashing around balcony doors. If the regional contractor offers a paid apprenticeship in equipment repair with actual vacancies, I'd enrol after seeing the machine work safely. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep my current wage until I had a written offer and put any extra seasonal pay toward the grocery card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years feels usable. I can learn with a skilled person beside me if the hours are paid. I will not buy a course while the mortgage is already tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the paid hours, who teaches the work and where the last group found jobs. A certificate alone will not bring a wage home. I left school with a trade certificate later on, and I learn best from a real repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the present job until an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few other builders near us, and my partner’s shop shifts are not full time. A promised opening could vanish before I start. My family needs the current pay, even if the rate is low.

I would ask what **paid jobs remain** after the demonstration.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots reach deck fitting.
Five years helps only if current **paid days** allow a savings buffer.

Keep the current wage until a **written offer**, then pay seasonal extras toward grocery debt.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to use a five-year warning for paid learning.
S3.quote: A certificate alone will not bring a wage home.
fieldNote: Liam will try **equipment repair** only after seeing safe work, paid instruction and actual vacancies.
His wish for more warning is tied to **present paid days**, not an imagined cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office changes by 2036 and robots reach our deck work around 2039. A decade should give builders time to show honest trials and apprenticeships with paid days. I would still ask about next season's cabin bookings before trusting a long plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can build the deck. Our children will be grown, so school pickup will not pin us to the same hours. I cannot assume retirement or a cleared mortgage while our pay remains low and the reserve is only weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid cabin work and use the AI app occasionally when a fastening mark is unclear, checking the approved drawing afterward. My partner and I would pay down the grocery card in good seasons, then try to save one month of bills. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask for a real deck-robot trial and contact regional builders if local bookings fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the coming lean season. The robot date is far enough away to plan, but winter pay is already close. I would feel better with a month of bills saved and a full season in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you commute farther after the children grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could try a longer commute before moving, if there were a paid offer. My partner and I would check fuel costs against the wage. Grown children make the school run easier, not the mortgage smaller by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help next season?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A booking list with enough paid deck days and prompt notice when weather changes a job. That would let us clear the grocery card and build a reserve. A robot demonstration cannot pay next winter’s bill.

I would still demand next season’s **cabin bookings** now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner’s shop work may change first and capable deck-building robots follow around 2031. Paid apprenticeships with actual openings, a real rotten-ledger trial and a full season of booked shifts would help. I will learn a proven tool, but my family needs wages while I do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the months between cabin projects. A long warning is easier to use when a worker earns a full season now. I would take paid work farther away if the offer and travel costs made sense.

headlineQuote: I will learn a proven tool, but my family needs wages while I do.
portrait: Liam is a **43-year-old certified** deck worker with experienced, average carpentry skills on holiday-cabin sites.
Low seasonal pay and part-time **farm-shop shifts** leave three weeks saved for a mortgage and two children.
He uses **AI occasionally** for plan marks, then checks timber, approved drawings and the site lead’s judgement.
He seeks **paid apprenticeships** and real regional offers while trying to build a one-month reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could affect farm-shop work before capable deck-building robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, actual openings, rotten-ledger trials and booked paid shifts would support his family.
